opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is really the vision behind what we've been calling hyper-representations, or learning on model zoos. The starting point is a simple observation: today, every time you have a new data set, you train a model from scratch, or you take some foundation model and fine-tune it. That's expensive, and in a way we throw away all the knowledge from the millions of models that have already been trained. Those weights are a data modality in their own right, and we haven't really treated them that way.

So what we did first was build large collections of trained models, model zoos, and train representation learners on the weights themselves, essentially autoencoders over neural network parameters. What we found is that the latent space is very structured. You can predict things like accuracy, generalization gap, or training epoch straight from the weights, without ever seeing data. And then you can sample from that space and generate new weights that perform well, sometimes better than what you'd get from random initialization, as starting points for fine-tuning.

The next step, and this is where your question comes in, is to make that generation conditional. Think of how text-to-image works: you give a prompt and the diffusion model produces an image. We want the same thing, except the prompt is your data set and the output is a set of model weights. So you take your private data, maybe a few samples or some embedding or summary statistics of it, encode that as the conditioning signal, and the generative model, trained on many data-set-to-weights pairs, produces a model that is already well suited to your task.

The privacy angle is important here. You may not want to, or legally be allowed to, send your data to some big provider to train or fine-tune a model. If all you have to share is a compact representation of the data, or if the generator runs locally, you never ship the raw data anywhere. You get a model tailored to your distribution with very little compute and without exposing the data itself.

There are open challenges, of course. Scaling from small CNNs to large transformers is non-trivial, because weight spaces have symmetries like permutations that you have to handle, and the number of parameters gets huge. We also need to understand how much information the conditioning really needs to carry and how well it generalizes to data sets far from what the generator saw. But conceptually I think it's a shift from training models to retrieving or generating them from the collective knowledge stored in all the models we've already trained.

r001.rationale: It describes conditioning a generator on a data-set representation to produce weights, but does not propose a shared embedding space aligning data sets and models like CLIP.

r002.rationale: It proposes encoding private data as a conditioning signal or prompt so a generative model produces task-suited model weights.

r003.rationale: It says a compact representation can avoid sharing raw data, but does not say the shared embedding conceals the individual samples it represents.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is really the natural next step from what we've been doing with hyper-representations. Let me back up a little bit. For the past few years we've been training models not on data, but on model weights themselves. We take populations of neural networks, we treat their weights as the data points, and we learn a representation space over them. And once you have that, you can do two things. You can go from weights to properties, so predict accuracy, generalization gap, hyperparameters, and so on. But you can also go the other direction. You can sample in that latent space and decode back into weights, and you get a working model out.

Now, the question becomes: what conditions the sampling? In the early work it was essentially unconditional, or we conditioned on a target property, like "give me a model with high accuracy." The idea with the data set as a prompt is that the condition becomes the data itself. You hand over a few examples, maybe a few hundred, from your private data set, and that acts as the prompt. The system embeds the data set, and the generative model over weights decodes a network that is already adapted to that distribution, without you ever running gradient descent on that data.

And the reason I think this is interesting, especially from a privacy angle, is that the mechanism looks a lot like what we see with in-context learning in language models. There you put examples in the context window and the model adapts its behavior without updating its weights. Here it's the inverse: the examples go in, and what comes out is weights. So you're trading the compute and the exposure of a fine-tuning loop for a single forward pass through a hypernetwork, if you like.

Practically, the way we approach it is we build a population of models trained on many different data sets, we encode both the data sets and the resulting weights, and we learn the mapping between them. Then at inference time, a new data set that the system has never seen gets embedded, and we sample weights conditioned on that embedding. The private data never has to leave the user's side in principle, because what you share is only the embedding, and the embedding is a compressed, learned summary rather than the raw samples.

I should be honest about where we are. This works nicely for small architectures and well-defined task families, like image classification on small data sets, where the weight space is modest and the population is dense enough. Scaling that up to larger models is where the open questions are, both in the generative model over weights and in how much information the data embedding actually carries. But conceptually I think it's a very clean picture: the data set is the prompt, and the model is the answer.

r001.rationale: The response says it encodes data sets and weights and learns a mapping, but it does not describe a shared embedding space or compare the approach to CLIP’s alignment of text and images.

r002.rationale: It explicitly proposes embedding a private data set and using that embedding to condition generation of model weights.

r003.rationale: It describes the embedding as a compressed summary and says raw samples need not be shared, but does not establish that the embedding conceals the individual samples it represents.

astra-6.text:
The idea would be to treat the data set itself as the conditioning input. Today, you give a model a text prompt and it generates text or an image. Here, you would give it examples from your private data set, and the output would be the weights of a model suited to that task.

To get there, you could learn from a collection of trained models and the tasks or data sets they were trained on. The question is whether you can learn enough of that relationship to generate useful weights for a new data set, rather than training a model from scratch every time.

For a private data set, you would ideally do that conditioning locally. Keeping the data private is a separate requirement; generating weights doesn’t automatically guarantee privacy. But that’s the vision: moving from describing what you want a model to do to generating a model that can do it.

r001.rationale: It describes learning a relationship between trained models and their tasks or data sets, but does not propose a shared embedding space or CLIP-like alignment.

r002.rationale: It proposes conditioning on examples from a private data set to generate weights, but does not specify using an embedding of that data set as the prompt.

r003.rationale: It says privacy is a separate requirement and local conditioning is desirable, but does not propose that a shared data set embedding conceal individual samples.

sol-6.1.text:
The idea would be to condition the generation of model weights on your private data set. Usually, we initialize a model and then optimize its weights on that data. Here, we’re asking whether a model that has learned about the space of neural network weights could propose a useful set of weights directly.

Of course, you wouldn’t feed an entire data set in as a text prompt. You would need some representation of it—perhaps an embedding that captures the task and the structure of the data. That representation becomes the conditioning input, and the output is a candidate set of weights for a specified architecture.

You’d still have to evaluate those weights on your task, and perhaps fine-tune them. But if the generated weights give you a good starting point, you could reduce the amount of training you need. And calling the data private doesn’t automatically make this privacy-preserving; where that representation is computed and what it reveals would matter.

r001.rationale: It mentions a data-set representation used to condition weight generation, but does not propose a shared embedding space aligning data sets and models like CLIP.

r002.rationale: It proposes using an embedding that represents the private data set as the conditioning input to generate candidate model weights.

r003.rationale: It notes that the representation could reveal information, but does not propose designing the shared embedding to conceal individual samples.
